title: The shoulder tap, before he turns
subject: couple
direction: Place him facing away down an open sightline and walk her in from behind — then stop directing. Tell him once, before she arrives: 'don't turn until you feel her hand, and when you turn, turn slowly.' Stand at forty-five degrees off his shoulder so you catch the turn and her face in the same frame rather than shooting his back. Say nothing at all from the moment she starts walking; the whole value of this frame is that neither of them is performing for you.
lighting: Open shade or soft late-afternoon backlight down the sightline, so the rim catches her veil as she approaches and neither of them is squinting into sun.
coaching: Photographers stand too close and get a clean turn but no anticipation. Back up and shoot wider than feels right — the empty space behind him before she arrives is what makes the picture read.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. The groom stands with his back turned in a sunlit garden; the bride approaches from behind and touches his shoulder for the first look. Full length, three-quarter angle, soft late-afternoon backlight through trees, shallow depth of field, natural skin texture, editorial wedding photography, 85mm

title: Foreheads together, eyes closed
subject: couple
direction: After the reveal, give them the quiet one. Both hands held between them at chest height, foreheads touching, eyes closed. Cue it as 'stay there a second and just breathe' rather than 'pose' — the instruction is to do nothing, which most couples find easier than being told where to put a hand. Shoot from slightly below eye level so the join of the two foreheads sits against clean background rather than against a busy horizon.
lighting: Large soft source from camera left, feathered so it wraps both faces evenly; keep the background a stop darker so the two heads separate.
coaching: One of them will smile and open their eyes to check on you. Say 'eyes stay closed, I'll tell you when' before you raise the camera, and then actually wait three or four seconds — the real stillness arrives after the nervous laugh.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. The bride and groom hold both hands and lean their foreheads together in a quiet private moment, eyes closed, half body framing. Soft window light from camera left, muted neutral background, shallow depth of field, natural skin texture, editorial wedding photography, 85mm

title: Silhouette kiss against the sun
subject: couple
direction: Put the sun directly behind them and drop your exposure until the sky holds colour and they go to shape. Their bodies must not merge into one blob — cue 'chests apart, chins together', so there is daylight visible between them at the waist. Get low, so their heads break the horizon line against open sky rather than against trees. Expose for the sky and let them fall dark; a silhouette with detail in the face is just an underexposed photograph.
lighting: Sun on the horizon directly behind the couple, no fill at all. Meter the sky, roughly three stops under the subject.
coaching: The gap disappears the moment they actually kiss and everything reads as one mass. Have them hold just short of contact — the silhouette reads as a kiss at a distance of an inch, and it keeps the shape legible.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. Bride and groom kissing in silhouette against a glowing orange sunset over open fields, full length, strong rim light outlining both figures, dramatic golden hour backlight, editorial wedding photography, 35mm

title: The lift that gets a real laugh
subject: couple
direction: Ask him to lift her only a few inches — not a carry, not a dip. The small lift is what produces the involuntary laugh, and the laugh is the photograph. Brief him quietly first so she doesn't know the exact moment. Position so the low sun rakes through grass behind them and flares slightly into the corner of the frame, and shoot immediately: you have about two seconds before the laugh becomes a pose.
lighting: Low sun behind and slightly to one side, flaring through foreground grass. A white bounce at chest height keeps their faces from going muddy against the bright background.
coaching: A big theatrical lift makes both of them tense and the faces go rigid with effort. Keep it small — feet barely off the ground — and it stays a moment rather than a stunt.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. The groom lifts the bride slightly off the ground and she laughs, golden hour sunlight flaring through tall grass behind them, full length, warm backlight, shallow depth of field, editorial wedding photography, 85mm

title: Walking away, veil in the light
subject: couple
direction: Send them away from you, hand in hand, and let them talk to each other. This is the frame you give when a couple is stiff — nobody can be self-conscious facing away. Tell them to walk slowly and not to look back until you call. Time the shutter for the moment her veil lifts and the sun passes through it, which happens on the stride, not between them.
lighting: Low sun ahead of them and slightly off-axis so it transilluminates the veil. No fill — the whole point is that they read dark against a glowing field.
coaching: They walk far too fast and are out of your working distance in four steps. Say 'slower than feels natural' and start shooting from the first stride, not once they're settled.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. Bride and groom walking hand in hand away from camera through a vineyard at golden hour, seen from behind, her veil catching low warm sunlight, full length wide framing, editorial wedding photography, 50mm

title: The ring exchange, over the shoulder
subject: couple
direction: You do not direct this one — you position for it. Get behind and just off the officiant's shoulder before the vows begin, so the hands are between you and the couple's faces. Focus on the hands, but frame so at least one face is in the frame behind them; hands alone are a stock photo. Move once, early, and then stay still: every step you take during vows is heard by the whole room.
lighting: Whatever the venue gives you. Meter for the hands, not the window behind — in a church the difference is three stops and the automatic reading will silhouette everything that matters.
coaching: Photographers frame too tight and lose the face, or too wide and lose the ring. Frame so the ring is on a third and the nearer face fills the opposite corner slightly out of focus.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. Close view of the ring exchange at the altar during a wedding ceremony, hands in sharp focus with the bride's face soft behind, warm church window light, shallow depth of field, editorial wedding photography, 135mm

title: The first kiss, from the centre aisle
subject: couple
direction: Be standing in the centre aisle, camera up, before the officiant finishes the sentence. This frame exists for about one second and there is no second attempt. Shoot wide enough to hold the whole altar and the guests' shoulders in the foreground — the context is what makes it a wedding photograph rather than a kiss. Fire a short burst: the first frame is usually the approach and the third is usually the break.
lighting: Ambient only. If the altar is lit and the nave is dark, expose for the couple and let the room fall away — that contrast is the picture, not a problem to fix.
coaching: Standing too far back turns it into a small event in a big room. Commit to the aisle, get closer than feels polite, and be back in your corner before the recessional starts.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. Bride and groom sharing their first kiss at the altar seen from the centre aisle, guests' shoulders blurred in the foreground, warm ceremony lighting, full length wide framing, editorial wedding photography, 35mm

title: The parents' faces during the vows
subject: family
direction: While the couple is speaking, turn around. The most emotional faces in the room are in the front row and nobody is photographing them. Find the mother of the bride first, then the father, then whoever is holding a tissue. Shoot from a low crouch at the end of a pew so you are not blocking a sightline, and use the longest lens you have so you never intrude on the moment you are taking.
lighting: Ambient. Front-row faces are usually lit by the same window as the altar, one or two stops down — check before the ceremony so you aren't chimping during the vows.
coaching: The instinct is to keep the camera on the couple the whole time. Give yourself a fixed rule — during the vows you are on the family — or you will never come home with this frame.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. The bride's mother watching the ceremony from the front row with tears in her eyes, half body, other family members softly out of focus beside her, warm ambient church light, shallow depth of field, editorial wedding photography, 135mm

title: First dance, room and all
subject: couple
direction: Shoot the first dance wide before you shoot it tight. Drag the shutter so the room lights record as warm shape rather than black, and put a single off-camera flash behind the couple as a rim so they separate from the dark floor. Keep the guests' silhouettes in the frame at the edges — a first dance photographed tight could be any two people anywhere. Move a quarter of the way around the floor between songs, not during.
lighting: Ambient drag at around 1/40, plus one bare off-camera flash behind and above the couple for rim. On-camera fill at minus two if the room is very dark.
coaching: Full front flash kills every practical light in the room and the picture looks like a school hall. If you only have on-camera flash, bounce it hard off a side wall and let the ambient do the rest.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. Bride and groom during their first dance in a dimly lit reception hall, warm string lights and guests silhouetted around the edge of the dance floor, rim light behind the couple, full length, editorial wedding photography, 35mm

title: Her face during the best man's speech
subject: bride
direction: Do not photograph the person speaking — photograph the person being spoken about. Set up opposite the top table with a long lens before the speeches start and stay there. The frame you want is the half-second between the laugh and the recovery, when she looks at him instead of at the speaker. Shoot in short bursts through the whole speech; there is no way to predict the line that lands.
lighting: Ambient. If the top table is backlit by a window, add a small bounce or accept the rim and expose for her face.
coaching: Standing beside the speaker gets you the speaker's gestures and the back of everyone's head. Commit to the opposite side of the room before the first speech and don't move.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. The bride laughing with her hand near her face during a wedding speech, seated at the top table, half body, warm reception lighting, shallow depth of field, natural skin texture, editorial wedding photography, 135mm

title: Her mother fixing the veil
subject: family
direction: Move the pair of them to the largest window in the room before this happens — the getting-ready room is always cluttered and lit by a ceiling bulb. Ask the mother to do the thing she was already doing, not to pose doing it. Frame so you see the mother's hands and the bride's face, which means shooting from the bride's side, slightly behind the mother's shoulder.
lighting: Big window at ninety degrees to the pair, sheer curtain closed if the sun is direct. Kill the room's overhead light — mixing tungsten with daylight on a white dress is a colour problem you cannot fix later.
coaching: The room's background is always a mess of bags and hangers. Spend thirty seconds clearing the frame before you raise the camera; nobody will remember you asked.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. The bride's mother adjusting her veil by a large window in a getting-ready room, half body, soft directional daylight, bride's face visible and calm, shallow depth of field, editorial wedding photography, 50mm

title: The bridal party, walking not standing
subject: bridal-party
direction: Never line them up and say cheese. Put them in a loose row, link arms, and walk them toward you across open ground while they talk to each other. Give one instruction — 'walk at the pace of the slowest person' — which stops the line from bending into a V. Shoot three or four passes; the second is always better than the first because they have stopped thinking about their feet.
lighting: Open shade or a high overcast, or backlight with the sun behind the line. Direct side sun across a row of six people gives you three squinting faces.
coaching: The line bends because the tall ones stride out. Put the tallest at the ends rather than the centre, and it self-corrects without you having to nag anyone.
prompt: Photorealistic professional wedding photograph. A bridal party of bridesmaids and groomsmen walking toward camera in a loose linked row, laughing and talking to each other, full length, soft overcast daylight, shallow depth of field, editorial wedding photography, 50mm
